questions.prompt: A user's record has active = true, locked_out = true, and password_needs_reset = false. Can this user log in right now?
options: No -- locked_out blocks login even though active is true; it's a separate gate from active, not a synonym for it
Yes, because active is true and that's the only field that matters for login
No, because password_needs_reset must be true before any user can log in
Yes, but only if they also hold the admin role
questions.explain: Lesson 1 teaches that active, locked_out, and password_needs_reset answer three separate questions -- locked_out blocks login independently of active, which stays true here.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the many-to-many join table that actually records which users belong to which groups is ________.
questions.explain: Lesson 2 names sys_user_grmember as the real table behind both the Group Members and Groups related lists -- a user can have many rows, and a group can have many rows.

questions.prompt: Match each term from Chapter 1 to what it actually is or does.
right: A scoped delegated-administration role for managing user records and group membership
The table storing every role record that exists in the instance
The join table tracking which specific users hold which specific roles
The related list on a role record defining which other roles it implicitly grants
questions.explain: sys_user_role is the table of role records; sys_user_has_role is the assignment join table; Contains Roles is the related list driving role inheritance; user_admin is a real out-of-box scoped delegated-administration role.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about ServiceNow's delegated administration roles, per Lesson 4.
options: user_admin manages user records and group membership but cannot touch catalog items
catalog_admin can manage the entire Service Catalog without needing the full admin role
report_admin is required before any user can view any report at all
A scoped role that sounds narrow can still be worth checking for its own Contains Roles list before granting it
Granting admin is always the safer, lower-risk choice whenever a request spans two administrative domains
questions.explain: user_admin and catalog_admin are each genuinely scoped grants, and the lesson explicitly says the habit of checking Contains Roles doesn't change just because a role sounds narrower. report_admin manages and administers reports platform-wide -- it isn't a prerequisite to merely view a report -- and the lesson explicitly calls defaulting to admin the opposite of safe, not the safer choice.

questions.prompt: In ServiceNow, when more than one ACL applies to the same operation on the same record or field, how do they combine to decide whether access is granted?
options: Every applicable ACL must pass -- one failing ACL blocks access even if every other one would have allowed it
Access is granted if any single applicable ACL passes, regardless of the others
Only the most recently created ACL is evaluated; older ones are ignored
The platform averages the pass/fail results and grants access on a majority
Table-level ACLs are ignored once any field-level ACL passes
ACLs combine only when a Business Rule explicitly merges their results
questions.explain: Lesson 6 establishes AND evaluation across every applicable ACL: if three ACLs apply and two pass but the third fails, access is still denied.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes what a new admin instinctively (and incorrectly) assumes -- an OR relationship. ACLs actually combine with AND: one failing ACL denies access even if every other applicable ACL would have passed.

questions.prompt: The contractor role passes both incident.read and incident.write (table-level). A field-level ACL named incident.caller_id requires the itil role, which this contractor does not hold. What does the contractor actually see when they open an Incident?
options: The full record except the Caller field, which is simply missing from their view -- nothing else is affected
Nothing at all, because failing one field-level ACL blocks the entire record
The Caller field, but shown as read-only text instead of hidden
An error message instead of the form, because of the ACL mismatch
questions.explain: Lesson 7's worked example: passing table-level ACLs admits the contractor into the record, while the independent field-level ACL on caller_id withholds just that one field, with nothing else broken.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the correct order for working any access-denied report, per the Lesson 9 troubleshooting workflow.
items: Identify the exact operation and field -- is this table-level or field-level?
Turn on the Security Debugger and reproduce the issue
Open the specific ACL the debugger flagged and check its role, condition, and script
Confirm the user's actual roles and group memberships against what the ACL requires
questions.explain: Lesson 9's repeatable order of operations: classify the symptom first, reproduce it with the debugger, read the exact ACL it flags, then confirm the user's real access rather than assuming it.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: to edit an ACL record itself, an admin must activate the ________ role through Elevate Roles -- it is deliberately not held permanently active, even for a full admin.
questions.explain: Lesson 9 explains that security_admin is powerful enough to bypass the very ACL evaluation it configures, so it's activated only for the session where it's deliberately needed.

questions.prompt: IT wants a "Report an Outage" form that, the moment it's submitted, should become a real Incident record directly, with no approval chain or fulfillment-task tracking needed. Which catalog object should this be built as?
options: A Record Producer (sc_cat_item_producer), targeting the Incident table
A standard catalog item (sc_cat_item), generating a Request and Requested Item
A Variable Set attached to the existing Incident form
A Catalog UI Policy scoped to the Incident table
questions.explain: Lesson 14: a Record Producer writes directly to a target table (here, incident) with no sc_request/sc_req_item layer at all -- exactly the case where the standard request-fulfillment lifecycle would be an unnecessary extra layer.

questions.prompt: Match each Service Catalog table to what it actually stores.
right: The table representing a storefront; most organizations use just one
The table defining a variable's label, type, and conditions -- not the requester's actual answer
The table storing every catalog item a requester can order
The self-referencing table building the parent/child browsing hierarchy
questions.explain: sc_cat_item stores catalog items; sc_category is self-referencing via a Parent field for subcategories; sc_catalog represents the storefront itself; item_option_new is the variable definition, distinct from sc_item_option which captures the requester's answer.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about catalog variables and Variable Sets, per Lesson 12.
options: A Reference variable points to a real record on another table instead of accepting free text
item_option_new stores the requester's actual submitted answer
A multi-row Variable Set lets a requester add repeated rows of the same group of variables on one form
A variable used identically across many catalog items should generally live in a shared Variable Set rather than being redefined on each item
Choice and Multiple Choice variable types work identically, with no real difference between them
questions.explain: The requester's actual answer is captured on sc_item_option, not item_option_new (which is the definition); and Choice allows exactly one selection while Multiple Choice allows more than one, so they are not identical.

questions.prompt: A newly built catalog variable called "Need by Date" isn't reacting to a rule meant to make "Rush Justification" mandatory when it's less than 3 business days away. The admin built the rule in the standard UI Policy list against the catalog item's underlying table. Why would this rule never fire?
options: Catalog variables live in item_option_new/sc_item_option, not as columns on the table -- only a Catalog UI Policy (catalog_ui_policy) can watch and react to them, not a standard UI Policy
UI Policies can only ever be built on the Incident table, never a catalog item
The rule needs a Business Rule instead, since UI Policies cannot reference date fields
Catalog variables can only ever be made mandatory, never made visible, by any policy type
questions.explain: Lesson 13: the two object types watch entirely different kinds of data -- a standard UI Policy has no way to see or react to a catalog variable, which is exactly why a separate catalog_ui_policy object exists.

questions.prompt: A notification is meant to tell a caller their incident was resolved, but testing shows the assignee receives the email and the caller gets nothing, even though the trigger correctly fires when State changes to Resolved. What's actually misconfigured?
options: The recipient ("Who will receive it") setting is pointing at Assigned to instead of Caller -- a setting configured independently of the trigger
The trigger itself is wrong and needs to watch a different field than State
The notification needs an Inbound Email Action before it can send to anyone
The Email Template is missing a field placeholder for the caller's name
questions.explain: Lesson 16: the trigger and the recipient are configured independently, and a correct trigger firing says nothing about who actually ends up as the recipient.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: ServiceNow matches a reply email back to its originating record using a hidden reference called a ________, embedded in the outbound notification and echoed back in the quoted reply text.
questions.explain: Lesson 18: the watermark is what lets inbound processing know definitively which record a reply is about, instead of trying to parse an editable subject line.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of the Lesson 19 Change Request notification flow in the order they actually happen.
items: A Change Request's State field is set to Scheduled, firing the notification's record-condition trigger
The assigned CAB group is resolved as the notification's recipients
The Change Notification email template renders with this record's real number, description, and scheduled dates
A CAB member replies, and the watermark in that reply is matched back to the same Change Request
questions.explain: Lesson 19's end-to-end trace: the trigger fires first, recipients resolve next, the template renders and sends after that, and only once the email exists can a reply's watermark be matched back to the record.

questions.prompt: What does a ServiceNow Data Policy (sys_data_policy2) actually enforce, and where?
options: A mandatory or read-only field rule enforced by the platform at the server, for every write path -- form, Import Set, Scripted REST API, or background script
A show/hide rule for a field, enforced only inside the browser while a form is open
A rule that can only ever run on the Incident table
A rule that silently deletes any record missing a required field, instead of blocking the save
A client-side script that overrides whatever a UI Policy already decided
A rule that only takes effect after Elevate Roles activates security_admin
questions.explain: Lesson 21 defines a Data Policy as server-side enforcement that holds no matter which door the write came through -- form, Import Set, REST API, or background script.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes a UI Policy (Lesson 20), not a Data Policy -- a UI Policy's show/hide behavior only ever runs in the browser on a rendered form, which is exactly the gap a Data Policy's server-side enforcement exists to close.

questions.prompt: A requirement says: hide the Vendor field unless Category is Software, and separately, require a Vendor value on every Software-category record no matter how it's created. Which statement correctly matches mechanism to requirement?
options: A UI Policy handles the hiding; a Data Policy handles the mandatory requirement -- no single mechanism can do both, since Data Policies never control visibility
A single Data Policy can handle both halves, since Apply to UI also controls visibility
A single UI Policy can handle both halves, since UI Policies enforce at the server as well as the browser
A Business Rule is required for the hiding, and a UI Policy for the mandatory requirement
questions.explain: Lesson 22: Data Policies never touch Visible/hidden behavior, so hiding Vendor requires an actual UI Policy, while guaranteeing the mandatory rule holds everywhere -- including non-form write paths -- requires a Data Policy.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Business Rule timing types, per Lesson 23.
options: A before Business Rule runs before the database write and can still modify the record being saved, or abort it
An after Business Rule runs once the write has already completed, and is typically used to update other, related records
An async Business Rule blocks the user's save transaction until it finishes, the same way a before rule does
A display Business Rule's job is to pass server-side data down to the client for the form's client scripts, not to write to the database
All four timing types only ever run when a user submits a form manually
questions.explain: Async is explicitly non-blocking -- the user's form submission returns immediately while it finishes separately -- and Business Rules fire on insert/update/delete/query regardless of whether a human filled out a form, so an Import Set or API write triggers them too.

questions.prompt: Match each Business Rule timing type to its real behavior.
right: Runs when the form loads, passing server-side data to the client before the page renders
Runs after the write, in the background, non-blocking, outside the user's save transaction
Runs before the save completes; can still modify the current record or abort the operation
Runs once the write has completed; commonly used to update other, related records
questions.explain: before can still change or stop the save itself; after fires once the write is done and typically touches other records; async does the same but non-blocking in the background; display exists only to hand server-side data to the client before render.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a script reads a system property's current value at runtime with the API call ________('property.name').
questions.explain: Lesson 25: gs.getProperty() is the real API a script uses to pull a property's current value, which is why an admin can change behavior later just by editing the property, with no code deployment.

questions.prompt: You need logic that sweeps every SLA record once an hour to catch any about to breach, with no single record edit triggering it. Which mechanism fits, and why not the alternative?
options: A Scheduled Job -- it fires because the clock expired, not because of a specific record event, and is built to operate across many records in one pass
A Business Rule -- it reacts the moment any SLA record is inserted or updated
A Catalog UI Policy -- it evaluates live in the browser as a form is filled in
A Data Policy -- it enforces a field rule at the server regardless of write path
questions.explain: Lesson 26's core distinction: a Business Rule is reactive to one record's event, while a Scheduled Job is proactive on a timer and typically sweeps many records at once -- exactly this scenario.

questions.prompt: A fulfiller reports SLA breach warnings now arrive 20-30 minutes late. Put the Lesson 28 diagnostic steps in the order you should actually perform them.
items: Check whether a System Property controlling the job's interval or batch size was recently changed
Review the Scheduled Job's 'Next action' field and its run history for whether it's falling behind schedule
Check the System Log around a specific run's start and end time for warnings or errors
Decide the fix based on which step actually surfaced the cause
questions.explain: Lesson 28's configuration-first order -- property, then schedule/history, then log, then fix -- because each step either rules out a cause or hands you the exact timestamp to search next.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the System Log application, per Lesson 27.
options: System Log > Errors filters syslog down to just error-level entries
System Log > Transactions shows web request-level logging, one entry per request processed
gs.error() writes a routine, informational message with no severity implication
The real troubleshooting workflow is to reproduce the issue first, then check the log around that timestamp
The System Log application is built on an entirely separate table from System Properties, with no shared architectural pattern
questions.explain: gs.error() is for an actual failure -- the most severe of the three calls, not a routine message (that's gs.info()) -- and the lesson explicitly draws the parallel that both the System Log views and Properties pages are filtered views over one underlying table.

questions.prompt: In the same session, an admin creates a new Business Rule and also creates ten test Incident records while an Update Set is active. Which of these changes actually lands inside that Update Set?
options: Only the Business Rule -- Update Sets capture configuration/metadata changes, never ordinary data records like a new Incident
Both the Business Rule and the ten Incidents, since both were created while the set was active
Only the ten Incidents, since Update Sets exist specifically to move data between instances
Neither -- Update Sets only capture changes made by an administrator with security_admin elevated
questions.explain: Lesson 29's boundary is customizations vs. data -- a new Incident is a data record and is never captured by an Update Set, regardless of which set is current.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: if an admin edits a Business Rule before creating and switching to their intended Update Set, that edit lands in the system's ________ Update Set instead, by default.
questions.explain: Lesson 30: every captured change goes into whichever Update Set is current, and if nothing else was made current first, that's the system's Default Update Set.

questions.prompt: Match each step of moving an Update Set between instances to what it actually does.
right: Actually applying the Update Set's changes to the target instance
Comparing every captured change against the target's current state before anything is applied
Saving a Completed Update Set as an XML file on the source instance
Uploading that XML file onto the target instance as a new, not-yet-applied Update Set record
questions.explain: Export saves the XML on the source; Retrieve loads it on the target as an unapplied record; Preview compares it against the target's current state; Commit is the step that actually applies the changes.

questions.prompt: Previewing an Update Set on Test flags that a Business Rule references a Script Include that doesn't exist yet on Test, because the Script Include lives in a different, not-yet-applied Update Set. What is this problem called, and what's the real fix pattern?
options: A missing dependency -- the fix is applying Update Sets to the target in the correct dependency order, so the referenced piece exists before anything referencing it is committed
A collision -- the fix is reviewing both versions side by side and choosing which one to keep
A skipped record -- the fix is documenting what was skipped and revisiting it later
A corrupted export -- the fix is re-exporting the Update Set from Dev and retrying
questions.explain: Lesson 32: a missing dependency is an absence (something referenced isn't there yet), distinct from a collision (a version mismatch) -- the real fix is dependency-ordered promotion, not choosing between two versions.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the Lakeview Facilities capstone build, per Lessons 35-36.
options: The estimated_cost field needed a field-level ACL, because a UI Policy alone only hides the field inside the browser and wouldn't block a report, Import Set, or integration from seeing it
The Relocation destination-location rule needed both a UI Policy and a matching Data Policy, since the UI Policy alone wouldn't hold if a record reached the table through an API integration
User records and group memberships created for Lakeview are captured and promoted by the Update Set along with the ACL and catalog item
The Furniture Request notification was built as an event-based notification rather than a condition-based one
A 30-day auto-close Scheduled Job scoped only to Incident would silently do nothing for the new Facilities Request table unless it was widened or a new job was added
questions.explain: Lesson 36 explicitly states user records and group memberships are not captured by an Update Set and must exist independently in each environment; Lesson 35 explicitly builds the notification as condition-based (State changes to Closed Complete), not event-based.

questions.prompt: Why was a field-level ACL the correct control for hiding Lakeview's estimated_cost field from staff, rather than a UI Policy alone?
options: A UI Policy only controls what a browser form shows; an ACL enforces at the data layer, so the field stays invisible to any report, Import Set, or integration too -- not just the form
UI Policies cannot be scoped to a custom table like Facilities Request at all
A field-level ACL is required any time a field uses the Currency type
A UI Policy would have deleted the field's value entirely, which an ACL does not do
questions.explain: Lesson 35 applies the same data-layer-versus-presentation-layer distinction Chapters 2 and 5 built toward -- hiding with a UI Policy alone leaves the value fully exposed to any non-form write or read path.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of the Lakeview Update Set promotion in the correct order, per Lesson 36.
items: Complete the Update Set only after every piece has been tested together in Dev
Move the completed set to Test, where someone other than the builder walks through a real Furniture Request
Retrieve and commit the same set in Production only after Test passes
If a missing dependency surfaces, fix it in Dev, re-test, and move a corrected set through the same path
questions.explain: Lesson 36's described order: complete in Dev, verify in Test by someone else, only then commit to Production, with any problems fixed back in Dev rather than hand-patched downstream.
